title: Dream staying focused and confident ahead of WNBA Finals Game 6 despite scheduling madness - CBS Sports
description: Down 3-2 in the series, Atlanta faces elimination at home on Thursday in a midday showdown against the Valkyries
body:
Down 3-2 in the series, Atlanta faces elimination at home on Thursday in a midday showdown against the Valkyries
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:30 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        ATLANTA -- While the Atlanta Dream and WNBA play the blame game and the outside world expresses outrage and condemnation over the midday Game 6 of the WNBA Finals, Dream players and head coach Karl Smesko are staying laser-focused on the task at hand: evening the series against the Golden State Valkyries and keeping their hopes of a WNBA championship alive."Funny thing about Atlanta, I knew they were going to show up and show out," Angel Reese told reporters on Wednesday afternoon after practice at Gateway Center, referring to the fact that the game sold out just hours after tickets became available on Monday. "It being sold out is not a surprise to me because I know how much they support us and they've supported us all season. So it is really cool, and I'm really grateful to be able to play in front of the fans one more time."Despite the scheduling debacle turning into a bigger conversation than the basketball itself, Smesko said the team hadn't really even talked about it that much among themselves. "I haven't really heard them mention much about it, so I think we're handling it great," the second-year coach said. "I think we're trying to focus on the basketball and let other people take care of that, and we're just glad that it came to a solution." 
Thursday will be a historic day no matter what. It will be the first Game 6 in WNBA Finals history -- the championship series just switched to best-of-seven in 2025, and the Las Vegas Aces swept the Phoenix Mercury in the first edition. Game 6 was originally scheduled at a more traditional time of 8 p.m. ET. The Dream, though, had only reserved their regular-season home, the Gateway Center Arena, for the playoffs. The problem? The Gateway Center Arena is the smallest in the league, seating only 3,500 fans. Five Dream regular-season games and all previous playoff games were played at State Farm Arena, the 17,000-seat home of the Atlanta Hawks. But last-minute scheduling changes made it possible to host Games 3 and 4 at State Farm, but the Hawks tip off at 8 p.m. at home on Thursday and weren't giving up their arena. That left this Thursday matinee -- 12:30 p.m., to be exact -- as the best option all parties could agree to.But while Dream ownership was calling out WNBA leadership, and others were throwing stones back at the Dream organization, the players had a much more immediate issue to deal with: the Valkyries' defense.
        
            
                Why is a WNBA Finals game starting at 12:30 p.m. on a Thursday? Everything to know as Dream blame the league
                
                    Jack Maloney                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
The Valkyries and Dream had the top defenses in the league this season, so it's not a surprise that scoring has been tough to come by in this series. But since the Dream won Game 3 97-91 to take a 2-1 lead in the championship round, the Valkyries have absolutely stifled Reese and her team, winning Game 4 in Atlanta 67-62 and Game 5 back in San Francisco 64-55. Reese, who was on fire earlier in the series, was held to just 15 points combined in the last two games. 
Reese, the third-year forward who was traded to the Dream from the Chicago Sky in the offseason and was just named to the first All-WNBA second team of her career earlier this month, said the team had a particularly good film session on Wednesday morning and was ready to come out strong on Thursday and force a Game 7 at the Chase Center on Halloween."We are able to see in film that a lot of these things are just us, like missing shots or turning the ball over, or just not being on our defensive principles," Reese said. "Just kind of figuring that thing out is really just keeping us together. Honestly, [Dream rookie guard Isabele Borlase] said it today; she was like, 'I felt really, really good after that film session,' and that's good coming from a rookie because there could be a lot of pressure, especially going off a two-game losing streak. So everybody's in a great mind space right now."When asked what advice she had for her team heading into such a uniquely timed game, veteran DeWanna Bonner said that time and place were pretty irrelevant.
"I don't think that they need any advice. It's just win or die," she said. "No matter what the timing says, you can't even worry about that because that's the least of our worries. We just need a court, ball, hoop. Once we start feeding into all that, I think that's something the media can do. That's something the fans can worry about. We've got our own things that we got to figure out."Bonner said that despite her team's offensive inefficiency in the series, they planned to keep shooting, no matter what."We haven't lost confidence," she said. "That'd be crazy to lose confidence."

title: Lane Kiffin shocked over kickoff time vs. Alabama, says SEC doesn't want LSU to win - CBS Sports
description: LSU got a rare afternoon game against Alabama in Death Valley
body:
LSU got a rare afternoon game against Alabama in Death Valley

        When the SEC announced kickoff times for its Nov. 7 games, there was some shock when Alabama vs. LSU was listed as a mid-afternoon game instead of a night game. Count Lane Kiffin amongst those who were surprised by that news. "I never even considered that it wouldn't be at night," Kiffin said when asked about the kickoff time during Wednesday's teleconference. For the last six seasons, the rivalry game between Alabama and LSU has been played at night. For the last time they didn't play at night in Baton Rouge, you'd have to go all the way back to 2010. "I didn't even think to think about the time," Kiffin said. "I just assumed, especially since the last 16 years, this game has been at night here all the time. I guess that's probably naive of me." 
The final twist of the knife was that Ole Miss, Kiffin's former employer, got the primetime slot for its home game against Georgia. In the wake of legal battles featuring Kiffin and LSU on one side and the SEC on the other, the LSU coach said it wouldn't shock him if the league office is trying to punish him. "I was joking to [LSU SID Michael Bonnette] earlier, saying obviously the SEC wanted to change it from how it's been to give LSU less of an advantage because of how well LSU plays at night and how intimidating it is to play here," Kiffin said. "I was like, 'If someone thinks the SEC wants us to win this year after what's been going on, they must've just been on Mars the last four months.' "I guess when I look at it that way, I'm not surprised." While it is a little surprising that a likely top-15 matchup featuring two of the biggest brands in the SEC won't be played at night, it's not the first time this happened. Just look at the last time Alabama and LSU kicked off at 3:30 p.m. ET. 
The year was 2019. Joe Burrow led No. 2 LSU into Bryant-Denny Stadium against Tua Tagovailoa and No. 3 Alabama. It was one of the most highly anticipated games of the 21st century, but it wasn't played under the lights in primetime.  LSU's nightmares vs. Alabama Tiger Stadium is often ranked among the best atmospheres in college football, but that's especially true at night. Death Valley becomes a black hole for opponents' hopes and dreams. That is, except for Alabama. The Tigers have played the Crimson Tide at night in Baton Rouge every other year since 2012, and the results have been bad. LSU is 1-6 in its last seven night home games against Alabama, and many of those results have been lopsided.

I understand that this year's team is more talented than most -- if not all -- of the teams listed in the table above, but Death Valley will still provide an edge with an ear-splitting atmosphere in the late afternoon.No matter what time this game is played, pressure will be on Kiffin to deliver a win, which could be the source of his frustration. LSU will have at least two losses on its resume, and losing to the Tide would make the team's College Football Playoff path extremely narrow.

body:
The Brewers will start Jacob Misiorowski as they try again for their first championship, while the Rays turn to Drew Rasmussen on short rest
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:50 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Tampa Bay Rays took their first step toward a baseball miracle with their 12th-inning comeback win over the Milwaukee Brewers in Tuesday's Game 4 of the World Series. That 4-3 victory means the Rays avoided the sweep and cut the Brewers' series lead to 3-1. That sets the stage for Wednesday's Game 5. Tuesday's escape for the Rays was obviously an essential one, as it was an elimination game. The win also nudged the Rays' chances of winning the series from "all but impossible" to "merely a longshot." Across all of Major League Baseball postseason history, 42 teams have been down 3-0, and only one – the 2004 Boston Red Sox – has come back to win the series in question. That is, history suggests the Rays had a mere 2.4% chance of pulling off the miracle comeback when they were down 3-0. Now, though, they're down 3-1. In all, 96 teams have been down 3-1 in a best-of-seven MLB postseason series, and 14 of them have clawed back to win the series. That particular data set says the Rays have a 14.6% chance of stunning the Brewers and winning this Fall Classic. Those aren't great odds, obviously, but they're much better than the odds the Rays were facing going into Game 4. Interestingly, teams down 3-1 have a .500 record in Game 5. Speaking of which, that brings us to three questions for Game 5 – the answers to which will determine whether the Rays can cut the Brewers' advantage to 3-2 and send the series back to Milwaukee. Let's get to it.
1. What's the pitching plan for the Rays?Here's the big one. Rays manager Kevin Cash wisely managed Game 4 for what it was: a must-win contest. That means you worry about tomorrow when tomorrow comes and tactically do everything possible to survive the elimination game. Tomorrow, though, has now arrived, and Cash must figure out how to deploy his pitching staff for another elimination game after using seven arms on Tuesday. Game 2 starter Drew Rasmussen will be going on short rest in Game 5, but what then? The most notable Game 4 decision was using Nick Martinez, who had been slated to start Game 5, in relief. Martinez worked two scoreless innings out of the bullpen and threw 33 pitches. It'll be another all-hands-on-deck affair on Wednesday, but just who those hands will be after Rasmussen is another matter. Griffin Jax started Game 4 for Tampa Bay and amassed 74 pitches, which presumably rules him out for Game 5. As for the traditional relievers, Cole Sulser, Steven Matz, and Garrett Cleavinger did not pitch on Tuesday and thus can probably expect to be used in Game 5. Bryan Baker and Kevin Kelly did pitch in Game 4 but they didn't pitch in Monday's Game 3 blowout loss, which means they're presumably available. Ian Seymour also didn't pitch in Game 3, but his 32-pitch workload in Game 4 may rule him out. Tyler Wells and Cameron Booser have each pitched two days in a row, but desperate straits in October may mean they'll be called upon again. As for Rasmussen, he's made short-rest starts before, but he was basically an opener in those outings, the last of which was in 2022. This, then, is something close to virgin territory for him. No doubt, Cash won't lean on Rasmussen for a long start even if he's cruising, but they could use some bulk from him given the shallow and probably tired bullpen. This will be Rasmussen's fifth start of the 2026 postseason. Across his previous four starts, he put up a 2.19 ERA and 2.57 FIP with 27 strikeouts and five walks in 24 ⅔ innings. 
In light of the maxed-out stakes involved, anyone who's even a remotely feasible option will probably tell Cash he's willing to pitch. As such, Cash's decisions on whom to trust and whom to assign the plurality of innings will be fascinating and perhaps determinative. 2. Will Jacob Misiorowski be in peak form?No such dilemmas are to be found for Pat Murphy and the Brewers, at least insofar as their Game 5 starter is concerned. Jacob Misiorowski, the 24-year-old NL Cy Young favorite and the hardest-throwing starting pitcher anyone's ever seen, on Wednesday will make his fourth start of these playoffs. Last time out, Misiorowski in Game 1 against the Rays went five innings and permitted only one run en route to picking up the win. "Miz" also enjoyed a velocity bump compared to his prior run of starts. 
        
            
                Jacob Misiorowski's moment? MLB's most electric starter can pitch the Brewers to their first title
                
                    Julian McWilliams                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
However, he was coming off 11 days of rest in that start, and for his Game 5 trip to the bump he'll be on the standard four days of rest. He's well into career-high-workload territory in 2026, so it remains to be seen whether the sizzle he showed in the series opener will be back for Game 5. The Brewers could use some length from him given how hard the bullpen worked in Game 4. 
3. Is Junior Caminero 100%?The Rays' best hitter and one of the richest power sources in all of baseball had to exit Game 4 in the 12th inning not long after reaching base on Joey Ortiz's throwing error. He did so because of an injury to his left foot. From afar, this seems like the kind of knock that would earn Caminero a few days off had it occurred in, say, June, but this is very much not June. "Junior, he's fine and obviously in the lineup today. Really impressive that he went first and third right there, very instinctual play," Cash said on Wednesday."He's been dealing with some lower extremity injuries, but there's a lot of guys that are nicked up right now playing through a lot and know that Cammy will be ready to go today."
The heart of the matter is whether Caminero will be in top form less than 24 hours after sustaining the injury. That's worth pondering in light of his ongoing power outage. Caminero this postseason has a respectable .717 OPS, but he has only one home run in 48 at-bats. That's after hitting a whopping 42 homers during the regular season and averaging one every 14.7 at-bats. It's quite possible that the Rays will need some customary thump from the hard-hitting 23-year-old if they're going to extend the series. That we shall see.

title: Big Ten caps NIL spending, mirroring Protect College Sports Act framework - CBS Sports
description: The Big Ten approved a rule on Wednesday that limits each school's investment in athlete NIL deals to $49 million
body:
The Big Ten approved a rule on Wednesday that limits each school's investment in athlete NIL deals to $49 million, as the Senate-approved college sports bill awaits a potential House vote
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:47 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        On Wednesday, the Big Ten announced that it is implementing a $49 million NIL spending cap for all its member institutions, effective immediately. The policy is designed to mirror the cap proposed in the Protect College Sports Act, which is still awaiting a vote in the House of Representatives.The new policy would split spending into two buckets. The first is the revenue-sharing cap set by the House settlement, which comes to $21.6 million. The second is a $27.5 million cap on third-party NIL spending, which includes entities like collectives."While we await the passage of the Protect College Sports Act, which has our full support, it is imperative our member institutions can begin to plan, budget and build their rosters approximating the act's economic structure," the Big Ten council of chancellors said in a statement. "Our institutions remain in full support of the Protect College Sports Act and this rule not only allows for a much smoother transition into the policies put in place by the act once it passes, but demonstrates our commitment to it."Under the Protect College Sports Act, schools would be able to spend roughly $50 million on athlete payments, but with some strings attached. The House settlement money would remain the same, but athletic departments could also use a retention fund of up to $22.5 million to keep players in-house and slow the transfer portal frenzy.
Finally, schools could spend $5 million that is reserved specifically for women's and Olympic sports.With the future of the Protect College Sports Act uncertain at the moment, the Big Ten is at least providing its schools with a framework for building financial plans for 2027 and beyond.The $49 million number is notable because Oregon and Ohio State are spending more than $40 million on football alone this year, according to CBS Sports. Michigan and USC aren't far behind, approaching the $40 million threshold as well.
Uncertain future for PCSAThe House of Representatives is currently on recess through the midterm elections, which take place on Tuesday. The House will reconvene several days later on Nov. 9.At that point, the PCSA could go to a vote, but there are questions about its viability in a lame-duck session. That makes the real deadline for a vote on Jan. 3, when a new Congress will be sworn in. Any bill that has not become law at that point dies and must start the process all over again."I'm not sure what the fight is going to be like in lame duck as they try to push this over the edge, especially if the House switches from Republican to Democrat," Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), an opponent of the bill, told CBS Sports. "Democrats should have a chance to really author a bill that corrects for a lot of the failings in this bill."
In addition to the lame-duck session, the other threat to the bill is changes that some lawmakers would like to see made before its passage. A segment of Republicans in Congress is pushing for a ban on classifying athletes as employees, and others want a hard cap on the number of international athletes in college sports.If the PCSA were to undergo any changes at this late stage, it would have to return to the Senate for another vote, further undermining its already slim chances of becoming law.

title: Tyrese Haliburton injury: Pacers star to miss weeks due to hamstring strain - CBS Sports
description: Haliburton missed all of last season due to an Achilles tear, and now he's back on the shelf after only four game
body:
Haliburton missed all of last season due to an Achilles tear, and now he's back on the shelf after only four games
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:42 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Tyrese Haliburton's return to the Pacers lineup after missing the entire 2025-26 season with an Achilles tear has hit a speed bump, as the All-Star guard deals with a hamstring strain four games into the year. Pacers coach Rick Carlisle said Wednesday that after meeting with doctors, Haliburton would be considered "week-to-week" with his hamstring strain and is unlikely to play in the next two weeks."It's not good news, but it could be worse," Carlisle told reporters (via the Indianapolis Star). 
Haliburton, who sat out all of last season after suffering a torn Achilles in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals, has been terrific for the Pacers in his return to the court, averaging 21.8 points, 9.5 assists and 4.5 rebounds per game on 51.6/37.0/86.7 shooting splits over Indiana's first four games. After hitting some clutch shots in the opener, Haliburton was overcome with emotion thinking about his journey back to the basketball court, and now he will have to find that patience once again as he waits for his hamstring to heal enough to play again. 
How will the Pacers deal with Haliburton's injury?The Pacers will be without Haliburton for a big game on Wednesday night against the 76ers, with games against the Heat, Nets and Hawks up on the schedule over the next week. Indiana will try to navigate that stretch not only without their star guard, but with Ivica Zubac and TJ McConnell as players also listed as out on Wednesday's injury report, while Andrew Nembhard is questionable with a neck/back injury. That's a considerable amount of Indiana's guard depth that either can't play or will be playing at less than 100 percent, along with their top center. That shifts Pascal Siakam back into a lead role offensively and forces the Pacers into more small-ball lineups with Obi Toppin at the five. 
For a team trying to get back into the conversation in the Eastern Conference after a lost season in 2025-26, seeing injuries pile up early in the year is extremely frustrating and disheartening. The Pacers were a half of basketball away from winning a championship when Haliburton tore his Achilles in Game 7 against the Thunder and have spent more than a year waiting to get him back to try to make the climb again. While Carlisle noted in a radio interview on Wednesday morning the hope was Haliburton's hamstring wouldn't be a long-term injury, soft tissue injuries always bring some concern. The Pacers will have to balance patience with the desire to not fall too far behind in a suddenly stacked East. Haliburton joins growing list of injured starsHaliburton's injury continues a frustrating trend in the early NBA season, which has seen a tremendous number of top players listed on injury reports. The list of stars currently on the shelf with injuries is staggering, with the likes of Anthony Edwards, Jalen Williams, Paolo Banchero, Kawhi Leonard, Jaren Jackson Jr., Chet Holmgren and Alperen Sengun all currently listed out for games on Wednesday night. That's not to mention players like Brandon Ingram, Jimmy Butler, Kon Knueppel and Kristaps Porzingis who have yet to make their season debuts. 
While it feels like an absurd number of injuries this early in the season, it's much closer to par for the course than the NBA would probably like to admit. Stars being injured has become a constant concern in recent years, but there isn't an obvious solution.The NBA schedule is often discussed as a reason for the volume of injuries, but this early in the season, it's hard to point to the wear-and-tear of an 82-game grind. Instead, it feels more like a byproduct of a style of play that pushes players to their limits. The speed of the game is tremendous now and players are pushing their bodies to play faster and more explosively, which raises the potential for injuries. That's an even harder thing to solve than schedule reform -- which the league and players aren't particularly interested in -- because playing with pace and maximizing possessions is proven to be the most effective style in the modern era.

title: Lewis Uvwo commits to Providence: Five-star center picks Friars over Kentucky, Baylor - CBS Sports

body:
Considered the best center in the 2027 recruiting cycle, Uvwo is the first major high school recruiting win for Bryan Hodgson at Providence
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:41 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Five-star center Lewis Uvwo announced his commitment to Providence, picking the Friars on Wednesday over Baylor, Kentucky and Cal on CBS Sports HQ. Landing Uvwo, the No. 7 overall player in the 2027 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, is a major recruiting win for Providence coach Bryan Hodgson, who is entering his first season at the helm of the Friars.Uvwo is the highest-ranked center and considered the best big man in the 2027 class."What stood out to me about Providence were the people, the culture, and the way they made me feel throughout the whole process," Uvwo told 247Sports' Eric Bossi. "I felt like they genuinely believed in me, not just as a basketball player but as a person. Providence has a great basketball history with room to create more history and go to heights never experienced at the school, and I welcome that challenge. I wanted to be somewhere I could grow, be challenged, and help build something special. I felt like it was the right place for me and my future."Uvwo took an official visit to Providence last month after visiting Kentucky, Cal and Baylor. Uvwo, who attends national powerhouse Prolific Prep in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, is only the third five-star recruit that Providence has landed in the 247Sports era.Uvwo joins Ricky Ledo (2012) and Kris Dunn (2012) as the highest-ranked commitments in Providence program history.
Uvwo's commitment to Providence is a significant recruiting win for Coach Hodgson. It establishes the Friars as a major force not only in the Big East, but nationally."Coach Hodgson separated himself through his craft and the fact that he has always been a winner," Uvwo added. "You can tell he knows the game, understands what it takes to build a successful program, and has a clear vision for where he wants to take Providence. His track record speaks for itself, and I believe in what he's building and the role he sees for me in helping the program succeed. 247Sports Director of Scouting Adam Finklestein calls Uvwo an "elite defensive prospect" in his scouting report.
"It starts with his physical tools. Standing at 6-foot-10 with a nearly 7-foot-6 wingspan, he has massive length. More than that though, he's also a tremendous athlete. He runs, jumps, and changes direction with ease and fluidity. His reactions are incredibly quick for a player with his dimensions, allowing him to flip his hips or bounce back up for secondary jumps. He's a cut 225-pounds and looks like he'll continue to add muscle without sacrificing any of his explosiveness. He's also an energy-giver who not only plays with the high-motor necessary to maximize those physical tools, but brings a rare sense of joy with him to the court."It shouldn't come as a surprise that Providence has become a big player in the high school recruiting space under Hodgson. In CBS Sports' report that broke down the NIL arms race in college basketball, Providence ranked in Tier 4, which is a budget range of $12.1 million to $15 million. In that tier, Providence was notably joined by other Big East foes such as Georgetown, Creighton, Villanova and Marquette, and other power-conference teams such as UCLA, Ohio State, Baylor and Alabama.

body:
Johnson, 70, is in his 37th year hosting the show, a staple of NBA coverage

                    at

                •

        Ernie Johnson announced on social media Wednesday that this will be his final season as the host of "Inside the NBA." The 2026-27 season is Johnson's 37th as the host of the popular pre- and post-game show featuring himself, Charles Barkley, Shaquille O'Neal and Kenny Smith, which has been a staple of NBA coverage since its debut in 1989."This will be my last season," Johnson said. "Totally my decision. It's just time. It's been an honor to share so many nights, decades actually, with my brothers."Although Johnson, 70, is stepping away from his role on "Inside the NBA" after this season, he will still be part of TNT and CBS Sports' March Madness coverage, he announced in a nearly three-minute-long video.
"Just to be clear, I'm not retiring," Johnson said. "Just cutting back. I'll still do March Madness and other projects for TNT and CBS, and I've just started a new production company called 32 Bowties geared toward telling feel-good stories in sports. So this is by no means the end. It's just a turning of the page. I'll forever cherish every chapter we have written with Inside the NBA."Barkley, who is a staple on "Inside the NBA," said last month on an episode of "The Bill Simmons Podcast" that this season would also be his last unless Johnson changed his mind to return beyond this season.
"Me and Ernie are a package deal," Barkley said. "Ernie said to me, 'Chuck, would you please stay for two more years?' I said, 'I love you, man. You're the best. I'll stay for two more years.' So right now, unless Ernie changes his mind, next year is my last year, 100 percent. … If he says he's done, I'm gone."

        Tight end Sam LaPorta's interview for "Pardon My Take" created a stir last week after the podcast aired. The 2023 second-round pick voiced frustration over the lack of progress on a new deal with the Detroit Lions, indicating he would be fine playing for another team next year. "Like last year, whatever it was, Week 9, Week 10, I break my f---ing back for the team. And then I'm going out there this year and I'm balling, and maybe they're just not showing the love," LaPorta said. "…I'm going to continue to do my thing and ball out, and in three months, if I don't get to wear the Honolulu blue and play for the Lions anymore, it's going to be all good. I'll go get paid somewhere else."A majority of the Lions fan base viewed LaPorta's comments as selfish, greedy, disloyal and tone deaf by airing his grievances publicly during the season. A few appreciated LaPorta's candor. Coach Dan Campbell seemed annoyed by being repeatedly asked questions about LaPorta's comments during a press conference last Friday. LaPorta later clarified his comments when meeting with the media. He stated that he prefers to remain with the Lions.
LaPorta was a non-factor in the Lions' passing game until the final drive during Sunday's 20-17 win over the Green Bay Packers. He finished with one reception for 18 yards on two targets. LaPorta isn't showing any ill effects from the herniated disc in his back, which he suffered nine games into last season, that required surgery, although it was his quietest game since early in the 2024 season. Despite the slow day, LaPorta is on pace for 79 receptions, a career-high 946 receiving yards and nine touchdowns.LaPorta is making $5.8 million in the final year of his four-year rookie deal. Contract extension talks between the Lions and Jack Bechta, LaPorta's agent, broke off about three weeks ago. The Lions are typically among the NFL's most proactive teams in locking up core players before their rookie contracts expire.Tucker Kraft's deal sets the baseline for Sam LaPortaBectha also represents Tucker Kraft, who is the latest relevant data point in the tight end market. Kraft, a 2023 third-round pick, received a four-year, $75 million contract extension from the Packers a day before the regular season started. The torn right ACL Kraft suffered during the middle of the 2025 season didn't deter the Packers from doing the deal. 
At $18.75 million per year, Kraft is the NFL's third-highest-paid tight end. Incentives and salary escalators totaling $17 million make this $18.75 million-per-year deal worth as much as $23 million per year. Kraft's 2028 through 2030 base salaries each increase by as much as $4.25 million annually based on his statistical performance, playtime and honors earned in the previous season. There are $4.25 million of incentives in 2030 also based on Kraft's statistical performance, playtime and honors earned during that season.For example, Kraft's 2028 base salary increases by $500,000 with at least 75 receptions in 2027. It's another $250,000 increase for hitting 85 receptions and an additional $250,000 for a total of $1 million with 95 or more receptions. Getting 800, 950, and 1,100 receiving yards generates the same escalation amounts. There are three levels with receiving touchdowns of at least seven, nine and 10 for $250,000 apiece. Having 80% or more offensive playtime is worth $500,000. Reaching 85% and 92% playtime is worth an extra $250,000, respectively. There's also a $250,000 increase for being selected to the Pro Bowl (on the original ballot) and another $250,000 for being named first team All-Pro by the Associated Press. It's the same criteria and dollar amounts as with the annual salary escalators for the 2030 incentives.Bechta is undoubtedly using Kraft's contract as a measuring stick for LaPorta. There is a parallel between the Christian Gonzalez/Devon Witherspoon situation and LaPorta's. The $33 million per year deal Reggie Johnson got from the Seattle Seahawks for Witherspoon in the middle of August to move the cornerback market set the table for Gonzalez, another one of his clients, to sign a $33.75 million per year extension with the New England Patriots, resetting this market again in early September as the start of the regular season was approaching.
LaPorta has been the more productive of the two tight ends. He set a single-season rookie record for a tight end in 2023, with 86 receptions, a record broken the following year by Brock Bowers. Those receptions went for 889 yards and 10 touchdowns.   LaPorta was named to the Pro Bowl and earned second-team All-Pro honors in the process. Kraft's career highs of 50 catches, 707 receiving yards and seven touchdown receptions were in 2024.LaPorta has 214 receptions for 2,438 yards with 23 touchdowns in 48 career games, while Kraft has 142 catches, 1,848 receiving yards, and 17 receiving touchdowns in 49 career games. Since entering the NFL in 2023, LaPorta ranks third and fourth, respectively, among tight ends in touchdown receptions and receiving yards.What a market-resetting LaPorta contract could look likeBectha is probably targeting more than just a nominal increase over his Kraft deal with LaPorta. It wouldn't be surprising for Bechta to look at how much of Kraft's performance bonuses LaPorta would earn based on him consistently performing like he did as a rookie in 2023. LaPorta's rookie season shouldn't be considered as a statistical outlier. His projected 2026 production is comparable to 2023's.
LaPorta would earn $86 million under Kraft's contract, using his rookie 2023 season as a baseline for future performance. A $21.5 million per year LaPorta deal would essentially be a 12.5% increase of the tight end market. George Kittle, another Bechta client, is the current standard with the backloaded four-year, $76.4 million extension averaging $19.1 million per year he signed with the San Francisco 49ers in April 2025. Presumably, Bechta is insisting on establishing new tight-end benchmarks for overall guarantees and for the amount fully guaranteed at signing. Those are Trey McBride's $43 million in the four-year, $76 million extension, averaging $19 million per year he signed with the Arizona Cardinals in 2025 about three weeks before Kittle and the $36 million in the three-year, $53 million deal Kyle Pitts, who was designated as a franchise player for $15 million, received from the Atlanta Falcons during June.It remains to be seen whether LaPorta's outburst will spur additional contract talks this season. Notwithstanding LaPorta's clarification, usually the longer a player incurs the risk of injury and poor performance in a contract year, the more he will want to test the open market unless his contract demands are met. That's something the Lions may want to consider with LaPorta.
LaPorta's comments prompted some media speculation that he could be dealt before the trade deadline. It should be noted that the Lions opted against making a substantial tight end investment in T.J. Hockenson. He was dealt to the Minnesota Vikings, an NFC North divisional rival, at the 2022 trade deadline instead. Getting rid of LaPorta this season would create a big hole in Detroit's offense. Tyler Conklin and Brock Wright are LaPorta's primary backups at tight end. Franchise tag could complicate Lions decisionDetroit balking at Bechta's demands could open the door to LaPorta becoming an unrestricted free agent in 2027. If the Lions plan on keeping LaPorta and fellow 2023 second-round pick safety Brian Branch, who just returned from the right Achilles tendon he tore late last season, one of two has to be signed to a new deal before the 15-day franchise tag designation period expires next March 3.Using a franchise tag would be a major departure for the Lions. The last usage was in 2018 on edge rusher Ziggy Ansah.
Under the NFL collective bargaining agreement's formula for non-exclusive franchise tags, the 2027 tight end number is projected to be 4.998% of the 2027 salary cap. That's slightly up from this year's 4.995%. The 2027 tight end franchise tag should be $16.169 million, with next year's salary cap being set at $323.5 million. A 7.4% increase in the salary cap over the current $301.2 million figure would be consistent with the 7.88% growth from 2025. If LaPorta is designated as a franchise player, he would have little incentive to do a deal quickly. Bowers will be eligible to sign a contract extension as soon as the 2026 regular season ends next January 10. He is the Las Vegas Raiders' primary receiving threat. LaPorta's best deal would come from letting Bowers massively reset the tight end market, provided it happened prior to the July 15 deadline for franchise players to sign long-term. Bowers' camp using the Raiders' 50% center market increase with Tyler Linderbaum to try to justify a deal in the $30 million-per-year neighborhood should be expected.
Highly productive tight ends in their prime rarely hit the open market. LaPorta will be 26 in January. Bechta would be licking his chops for the chance because LaPorta would be a hot commodity on the open market.

title: NBA rumors: Why one surging star makes sense as Thunder trade target - CBS Sports
description: There are future Hall of Famers and All-Stars who once donned the OKC uniform, but would it make sense to bring t
body:
There are future Hall of Famers and All-Stars who once donned the OKC uniform, but would it make sense to bring them in?
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:37 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            9 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Last season, a total of 11 players gave the Oklahoma City Thunder at least 900 minutes of service. Three of those players now play for other teams: Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe. Two of them, Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace, have already suffered injuries that may end their seasons. Another, Alex Caruso, has a sprained ankle. For Wednesday's game against the Dallas Mavericks, Chet Holmgren is also out with right knee patellar tendinitis and Ajay Mitchell is questionable with a right ankle sprain. In other words, most of Oklahoma City's core rotation from a year ago, aside from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, is not available right now. Inevitably, that has sparked quite a bit of speculation. The Thunder are as asset-rich as any team in the NBA. They have the picks to go trade for a difference-maker and a roster spot to add a free agent. The question here is who, and on Wednesday, ESPN's Brian Windhorst stirred the pot with an intentionally cryptic rumor."And this is one thing that I've talked to executives about, and I don't mean to be cryptic, but I'm being cryptic," he said on his Hoop Collective podcast. "If you're going to, if they're going to acquire a player, it would not be a surprise if they acquire a player they've already had."This makes plenty of sense on paper. The Thunder are very particular about their culture. Bringing in someone new is far riskier than reacquiring someone they already know, and given their asset surplus, they can afford to be picky. Given Windhorst's track record of cryptic reporting leading to seismic transactions, let's take a look around the league to see which former Thunder players, if any, make sense as reacquisition targets.
The illegal targetsThe Thunder traded Dort, Joe and Wiggins last offseason. Given how things have played out, Oklahoma City may regret doing so, and given this rumor cycle, fans will inevitably call for them to try to reacquire one of last season's core pieces. Alas, Dort, Joe and Wiggins are functionally not obtainable to the Thunder. The NBA does not allow teams to reacquire players they have traded until the following season. That means Dort, Joe and Wiggins are off limits for now.There is a very narrow exception to this rule, but it is not likely to come up. If the player is traded a second time and then gets waived, the original team can re-sign him upon clearing waivers. This happened with Mike Conley and the Minnesota Timberwolves last season. Of course, no team is likely to waive Dort, Joe or Wiggins, so we should assume for the sake of argument that they are off the table.
        
            
                What Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace injuries mean for the Thunder and why a trade isn't so simple
                
                    Sam Quinn                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
The impractical targetsThe Thunder have been so well-run for so long that the NBA is now littered with extremely accomplished Thunder alumni. Of course, these players are, in most cases, either so expensive that they would be impractical for Oklahoma City's purposes or so vital to their existing teams that they likely are not functionally available. So let's roll through those players now:
Domantas Sabonis and his $45.5 million cap figure are simply too pricey for an Oklahoma City team that is deepest in the front court.Kevin Durant is essential to a Houston Rockets team that, right now, probably has similar or better championship odds than the Thunder, so don't expect him to be available through trade. Besides, he's never exactly conveyed a desire to return to Oklahoma City.Jerami Grant is a useful player who suits Oklahoma City's positional need at forward. However, at $34.8 million, he simply makes too much money to be proactively targeted. The Thunder would have to give up one of their five most expensive players (Gilgeous-Alexander, Williams, Holmgren, Caruso or Isaiah Hartenstein) to match his salary, and that is presumably a non-starter for a player like Grant.James Harden, aside from being too expensive, just doesn't fit Oklahoma City's playing style. Gilgeous-Alexander is just a far better primary creator at this point, and Harden's defensive deficiencies would be problematic for a team that's built around defense.Steven Adams is plausibly affordable for the Thunder financially, but is impractical because he plays in Houston, plays their position of greatest depth, and has quite a few injury concerns of his own.The former All-StarsThe players listed above are all currently under contract with teams trying to win today. There are, however, quite a few famous Thunder alumni who are theoretically much more gettable. Four stand out:Russell Westbrook
A reporter asked general manager Sam Presti on Monday about potentially bringing back retired team legend Russell Westbrook. Presti gave a typical non-answer. Fans would certainly love to see Westbrook in a Thunder uniform again, but the question here is whether he'd be able to accept a small enough role for this to be worthwhile. Westbrook, who announced his retirement in August, is a high-usage player whose value is mostly derived from having the ball in his hands. His issues as a shooter are well-documented, and while he's capable of the sort of intense on-ball defense the Thunder prefer, he's never been consistent as a team defender. All in all, Westbrook is probably just too high-maintenance an addition given what the Thunder could expect out of a 37-year-old.Chris Paul
The point guard Westbrook was once traded for, Chris Paul, makes a bit more sense. He and Gilgeous-Alexander thrived together during the 2019-20 season. However, Paul fell off a cliff during his brief return to the Clippers last season, and he's a notoriously demanding locker-room presence. He's now 41 and has shown no interest in playing in the NBA again after announcing his retirement in February, so we can probably cross him off the list.
Victor Oladipo
Here's a sneaky one: Victor Oladipo. He spent this offseason trying to fight his way back onto an NBA roster. The Sacramento Kings worked him out, but did not sign him. He has not played since the 2022-23 season, but is still only 34. The healthy version of him fit into Oklahoma City's defensive culture, and after several years out of the league, he'd likely be happy with any role the Thunder could offer him.Al Horford
The only non-guard in this section: Al Horford. The Thunder, again, have plenty of front-court depth. If they did elect to trade one of their bigs for help elsewhere, though, Horford is still useful in a smaller role and the Golden State Warriors simply aren't competitive enough to turn away offers for players in their 40s. The Thunder have several trade exceptions big enough to fit Horford, and his salary is just below the $6.9 million in second-apron space they currently have available.Probably not sensible or cost-effective, but can't be ruled outAny of these three players theoretically could have landed in one of the last two categories. For reasons I'll explain, I wanted to separate them:

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Paul George 
George is more expensive than any player we've covered thus far. The only scenario in which this would make sense is one in which the Thunder trade Jalen Williams to Boston (along with a few other contracts, for the sake of legality). That, obviously, is enormously unlikely. It just isn't so crazy that it should be taken off the table altogether. The Celtics already showed a willingness to take a step back this season in the name of the longer view when they traded Jaylen Brown for George in the first place. The Thunder, however, have much more at stake this season given their impending financial cliff. George, with his player option, could actually help on that front by potentially renegotiating a slightly longer deal that suits the Thunder's needs. There would have to be draft picks going to Oklahoma City, and George would have to be willing to take a team-friendly contract that pays him less than Williams is due next season. But if you squint hard enough, you can see something that sort of makes sense here.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Josh Giddey 
The Thunder traded Giddey in part because his shooting made him an iffy off-ball fit next to Gilgeous-Alexander. Well, Giddey has made at least 38% of his catch-and-shoot 3s since coming to Chicago. The Bulls have a new front office that didn't bring Giddey in, and he's struggled to start this season. That doesn't mean they'll give up on him, but it means he could be gettable at the right price. Alas, price is the biggest hurdle here. The Thunder have no obvious way to cobble together the $25 million in tradable salary they'd need to match Giddey's contract without incurring an untenable first-apron hard cap. This would have to be a part of something bigger we can't foresee, so it's unlikely, but if the Thunder do something surprising, there might be a pathway here.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Dennis Schröder 
The Thunder could fit him into the trade exception they have leftover from sending out Dort, though they'd have to shed money elsewhere to duck the second apron. Schröder would likely be gettable for second-round picks later in the season (especially if Charlotte rookie Christian Anderson shows he can handle real minutes), and he'd simply be a spare ball-handler on point-of-attack pest defensively. He wouldn't have a big role in Oklahoma City, but the Thunder know him and what he brings to the table. Truthfully, though, the Thunder would probably just prefer to stick with what they have... unless things get worse.
The two best fitsAlright, we've spent the bulk of this story writing about players who wouldn't fit. Let's talk about the players who could. There are two standouts here:
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Ousmane Dieng
The Thunder ironically chose Dieng one selection ahead of Williams in the 2022 NBA Draft, but Williams outplayed him and Dieng could never find a role in a crowded Thunder rotation. That rotation is less crowded now, especially at forward, and Dieng took advantage of all of the extra playing time he got for the Milwaukee Bucks after the trade deadline last season. Dieng has held a much smaller role for the Bucks this season, so he's theoretically gettable. He can't be traded until Dec. 15 because he just signed a free agent contract, but the Thunder likely don't want to rush into a move anyway.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Ty Jerome
This is the likeliest big swing on the table for Oklahoma City, if any is even possible. Jerome is in the middle of a breakout season for the Memphis Grizzlies and could be well on his way to an All-Star selection. He's also 29, has serious durability concerns, and is functionally on an expiring contract considering his player option. If the Grizzlies view this as a flash in the pan, or a chance to sell high on someone they don't want to give a big contract to next summer, the Thunder could be their chance. His cap figure is only around $9 million, so he's very obtainable. His shooting makes him an easy fit on any roster, and the Thunder have quite a bit of experience managing the workloads of high-impact players with durability concerns like Alex Caruso. 
Jerome is a bit duplicative of Ajay Mitchell, but beggars can't be choosers. If the Thunder have to reorient their roster more around offense to maintain this season's title window, they should do so. Oklahoma City has enough of a draft surplus to trade for even an expensive rental. The question simply comes down to whether or not the Grizzlies view Jerome as a long-term fixture or a pleasant surprise they're willing to cash out. The former is likelier, but we can't rule out the latter.

A 3-17 record across two seasons and an offense that ranked last in Conference USA proved to be Longo's undoing with the Bearkats

        Sam Houston has fired coach Phil Longo after less than two seasons, the school announced on Wednesday. Associate head coach Eric Raisbeck and defensive coordinator Freddie Aughtry-Lindsay will serve as interim co-head coaches for the rest of the season. Longo went 3-17 in two seasons, including 1-11 in Conference USA play. The Bearkats are winless against an FBS opponent and lost 24-3 to Missouri State on Tuesday, their ninth straight against FBS competition. "Phil has contributed to Bearkat football as both an offensive coordinator and head coach, and we appreciate his work with our student-athletes," athletic director Bobby Williams said in a statement. "Our responsibility is to evaluate the program's performance and direction. After careful review, I believe a change in leadership is necessary to position Bearkat football to compete consistently in Conference USA and meet the expectations of our student-athletes, university and supporters." Longo was hired for his first FBS head coaching role only weeks after he was fired as Wisconsin's offensive coordinator, making him a cheap addition for a young FBS program. He was hired to replace K.C. Keeler, who led the Bearkats to an FCS national championship in Spring 2021. Under Keeler, the program went 10-3, with its first bowl win since transitioning to FBS two years earlier. 
Longo worked as an offensive coordinator under Keeler from 2014-16, helping to lead the program to two Southland titles and a national FCS semifinal. But from the start, Longo struggled to find his way with the Bearkats. His signature offense ranked last in CUSA both seasons as a head coach, including a paltry 322.8 yards per game in 2026. The Bearkats scored only three points in three of their four conference games.

title: Jaguars, Lions set to unveil a new uniform in Week 8 with 'Rivalries' set - CBS Sports
description: The Lions and Jaguars will both be debuting new uniforms on Sunday
body:
The Lions and Jaguars will both be debuting new uniforms on Sunday
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:22 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Two NFL teams will be debuting a totally new look on Sunday, with the Detroit Lions and Jacksonville Jaguars both getting set to play in their "Rivalries" uniforms for the first time. The Lions will be rocking their uniforms in an NFC North showdown with the Vikings, while the Jaguars will unveil their new look against the Colts. The Jags and Lions will both be playing at home on Sunday, and both games will kick off at 1 p.m. ET. The new uniforms were actually unveiled back in August, but the two teams haven't gotten a chance to wear them just yet. Both uniforms were designed as part of the NFL's "Rivalries" program. The idea was to create a new look based on a theme that's local to each team. The Lions teamed up with Nike to create a "Defend the Den" uniform featuring a white jersey, white pants and a Honolulu blue helmet.
According to the team, the blue helmet features "Carbon fiber within the decals texture symbolizes elite performance and connects to Detroit's car and racing culture."On the Jaguars' end, their new uniform is an ode to the city of Jacksonville and Duval County. The Jags' helmet has "Duval" written on the back bumper, while on the front end, the team added Jacksonville's "904" area code. If you watch the Jags play on Sunday, the helmet will probably be the first thing you notice. Jacksonville will be wearing a teal helmet for the first time in franchise history. 
As for the rest of the uniform, the Jags didn't get too crazy. They'll be wearing a white jersey paired with black pants. 
The font used for the numbers was "heavily inspired by the historic music venues and southern rock influence that Jacksonville is known for," according to the team. The Jaguars and Lions won't be the first teams to wear their new "Rivalries" uniform this year, and they won't be the last. All four teams in both the AFC South and NFC North have unveiled new uniforms, but so far only the Colts and Packers have worn them. 
The Colts wore theirs during a win over the Texans in Week 3. 
As for the Packers, they debuted their new look during a 31-7 win over the Bears in Week 5. 
The Packers' win means teams are 2-0 this year when wearing their "Rivalries" uniforms. Here's the full "Rivalries" schedule for 2026. Keep in mind that with the games below, only the home team will be wearing the new uniform: 
Week 8 (Nov. 1): Vikings at Lions, 1 p.m. ET (Fox)Week 8 (Nov. 1): Colts at Jaguars, 1 p.m. ET (CBS)Week 10 (Nov. 15): Jaguars at Titans, 1 p.m. ET (Fox)Week 11 (Nov. 19): Colts at Texans, 8:15 p.m. ET (Amazon)Week 15 (Dec. 20): Lions at Vikings, 8:20 p.m. ET (NBC)Week 16 (Dec. 25): Packers at Bears, 1 p.m. ET (Netflix)Each team will only wear their "Rivalries" uniform once this season, but they'll be allowed to keep it in their rotation for the next three years. The teams in the AFC East and NFC West kicked things off in 2025 when they became the first ones to get a "Rivalries" uniform. The program will run through 2028, and by that point, all 32 teams will have unveiled their new look. Here's when each division will be getting their "Rivalries" uniform: 2025: AFC East and NFC West (See all the 2025 uniforms here)2026: AFC South and NFC North (See all the 2026 uniforms here)2027: AFC West and NFC East2028: AFC North and NFC SouthWe'll have to wait two more years before we see the full set of 32 uniforms, but so far, it seems like the teams have been fully embracing the concept.

body:
We're closer to learning which team will have the ability to potentially draft USC star JuJu Watkins at No. 1
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:01 pm ET

            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The 2027 WNBA Draft Lottery will take place on Sunday, Nov. 15, the league announced Wednesday, and will air at 7:30 p.m. ET on ESPN after the UConn vs. Louisville women's basketball game. With that announcement, the WNBA revealed the official odds for the new seven-team lottery, headlined by the new edition of the Houston Comets (formerly Connecticut Sun) and the Toronto Tempo, who will split the best odds for the No. 1 overall pick.  The WNBA uses two-season aggregate records to determine lottery odds, but for the two expansion teams, the Tempo and Portland Fire, only their 2026 record will be considered. The Comets (as the Sun) went 22-66 over the last two seasons, while the Tempo were 11-33 in their inaugural campaign.  Because the two teams went 11-33 and had identical .250 winning percentages, the league combined each team's lottery combinations and divided them evenly. There was an even number of combinations, which means the teams will have identical odds for the No. 1 overall pick. If there had been an odd number of combinations, the Comets would have received the extra combination by virtue of losing the tiebreaker last season. In addition to the Comets and Tempo, this year's lottery crew includes the Chicago Sky, Seattle Storm, Phoenix Mercury and Los Angeles Sparks. However, those will not be the seven teams drafting in the lottery.
